brief.head: Moth in disguise
brief.text: A moth in a poi­sonous insect’s colours is iso­mor­phic mimicry, Ajay Shah said: an agency full of pomp, empty in­side. In the other fail­ure, the in­side is staffed but mal­func­tions. {082-C02}

brief.head: Born with a watchdog
brief.text: Every American fed­eral agency has an in­spec­tor gen­eral who can in­ves­ti­gate its high­est bosses, Ajay Shah said. Built over a hun­dred years, it is sim­ply taken for granted. {082-C04}

brief.head: STEM is the easy bit
brief.text: Technical knowl­edge has a fi­nite set of books and can be ex­am­ined, Ajay Shah said. “What exam is going to test that you un­der­stand epis­te­mol­ogy?” {082-C08}

brief.head: Plan for the worst
brief.text: The state should be de­signed so the worst ruler can do lit­tle dam­age, Amit Varma said. Ajay Shah said every health­care ex­pert must trace the fail­ures back to the con­sti­tu­tion. {082-C13}

brief.head: More calls that work
brief.text: Economic de­vel­op­ment, Ajay Shah said, is an ever-expanding range of pub­lic-goods ca­pa­bil­i­ties, pri­vate con­tract­ing and con­tract en­force­ment, so that more com­plex firms can take root in India. {082-C15}

thought.label: Thought for the day

thought.who: Ajay Shah, warning against the modern temptation to over-specialise

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah on why good policies fail to travel
lead.head: Lost in transplantation

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 82

body: A pol­icy that works in Norway or France will not nec­es­sar­ily work in India. The rea­son, Ajay Shah ar­gued, is in­vis­i­ble in­fra­struc­ture: the hun­dred other sys­tems on which any pol­icy qui­etly de­pends.

Amit Varma, who has been urg­ing his co-host to write a book on the idea, opened by wel­com­ing lis­ten­ers to *The Seen and the Unseen*. No, he added, this was not a cross­over: the episode was sim­ply about un­seen things.

Shah began with a mil­i­tary af­fairs geek who falls for the Norwegian mil­i­tary and wants to bring its man­u­als and pro­ce­dures to India, or an ad­mirer of TSMC who would repli­cate it in Bombay. “And the thing is this stuff doesn’t work,” he said.
## Blind spots

The sup­port­ing sys­tems are not hid­den, Shah said. Courts, the rule of law, prod­uct li­a­bil­ity, gov­ern­ment HR and con­tract­ing are all there to be seen. They are in­vis­i­ble be­cause spe­cial­ists do not look at them. {082-C01}
“If you only bother to look, all the things are there,” he said. “But the thing is that the peo­ple who are spe­cial­ists tend to be blind about them.”

He of­fered a soft­ware anal­ogy. Every in­sti­tu­tion makes API calls to ca­pa­bil­i­ties it does not own: a mil­i­tary calls on pen­sions, a hos­pi­tal on prod­uct li­a­bil­ity and the courts. In rich coun­tries the calls re­turn. Under un­der­de­vel­op­ment, they fail or work only some­times. {082-C03}

Court calls make the point. A med­i­cal mal­prac­tice case in the UK, Shah guessed, has about an 80 per cent chance of being de­cided cor­rectly. In India it is “al­most a coin toss”, and the mess re­shapes the whole health­care sys­tem.

Privacy shows the cost of ig­nor­ing all this. Advanced economies spent the 20th cen­tury build­ing checks on the state, so Western blogs worry about Google’s tar­geted ads, which Shah con­sid­ers a triv­ial prob­lem. Indians who learnt pri­vacy from those blogs car­ried the de­bate in the wrong di­rec­tion. {082-C06}
“In the Indian con­text, there is only one prob­lem to solve,” he said. “How to shut down state ac­cess to in­for­ma­tion about the peo­ple.”

Seasoned prac­ti­tion­ers are no cure. Someone with twenty years at the Bank of England, Shah said, bor­row­ing from Lant Pritchett, knows as much about pol­icy de­sign as a New York taxi driver knows about how cars work.
## What is to be done
Shah’s reme­dies began with a warn­ing: be wary of spe­cial­i­sa­tion. Narrow depth is the easy path and makes you less use­ful. Breadth is harder.
Next, he rec­om­mended “an ob­scure YouTube show by Amit Varma and Ajay Shah”.

Then take pub­lic choice the­ory se­ri­ously. Don’t as­sume the French doc­tor or the Norwegian gen­eral is a good guy. Ask why the doc­tor won’t over­pre­scribe for a kick­back from the X-ray clinic, and the an­swers will lead to the in­vis­i­ble in­fra­struc­ture.
Think lo­cally: be­fore trans­plant­ing French health­care into Haryana, know whether a truck car­ry­ing ex­pen­sive goods can travel a given road at night.
Sometimes, do noth­ing. State ca­pa­bil­ity, Shah said, is a very fi­nite mus­cle, and many times the wise an­swer is to shrink the scope of the Indian state. {082-C11}
And fix the foun­da­tions every sec­tor stands on, gov­ern­ment HR above all: fix it ev­ery­where, Shah said, and hun­dreds of agen­cies will work bet­ter. {082-C14}
## The last word
The episode ended on a joke from Shah’s list. “And also the YouTube shows that ex­pand the dis­course,” Varma said. “How could you for­get that?”
Shah agreed. “To get to those three things, you need great YouTube shows.”

second.label: The name of the show
second.head: Name that tune
second.deck: Two favourite songs offered titles; one phrase also described how the hosts think
body: When Amit Varma and Ajay Shah were choos­ing a name for their show, they took two can­di­dates from favourite songs. One was John Lennon’s *Watching the Wheels*. {082-R10}
The other came from Bruce Springsteen’s *You’re Missing*. Varma picked its phrase, ev­ery­thing is ev­ery­thing, and Shah said that the song res­onated with him too. {082-S07}

Varma told the story while riff­ing on C.L.R. James: “What do they know of cricket, who only cricket know.” James, he had re­cently found, was him­self riff­ing on Rudyard Kipling. {082-J11} Swap cricket for any word, Varma said, and the line holds. That, he said, is re­ally why the show is called *Everything is Everything*.

quote.text: When we put the songs aside, ev­ery­thing is ev­ery­thing just made sense be­cause that’s how we try to think about the world.

third.head: Driving isn’t designing

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the New York taxi driver

body: Lant Pritchett, Ajay Shah said, has an anal­ogy for the sea­soned first-world prac­ti­tioner. A New York taxi driver knows how to sit in a car, turn the steer­ing wheel and press the brakes. {#taxi}

He doesn’t know why cars are built as they are, or what trade-offs shaped the brakes. A vet­eran of the Norwegian mil­i­tary like­wise takes for granted five hun­dred years of lib­eral democ­racy, in which an Armed Forces Special Powers Act is unimag­in­able.
Or take twenty years at the New York Fed. “They know the how. But they don’t know the why,” he said. “And the why is an in­cen­tive story.” {082-S03}
Yet Indians, Shah said, lend such peo­ple in­sti­tu­tional le­git­i­macy be­cause they have worked twenty years at the Bank of England. “The an­swer is no.”

p2.title: What lies beneath
p2.deck: Ajay Shah on the systems every policy rests on, and what India should do about them. {082-C01}

quote.text: So here you have some­thing that doesn’t work in prac­tice, and so we should un­der­stand why it doesn’t work in the­ory.

box.title: The paper behind the idea
box.text: Amit Varma pointed to *Premature Imitation and India’s Flailing State* by Shruti Rajagopalan and Alex Tabarrok, which makes much the same ar­gu­ment. The term flail­ing state, he said, is taken from Lant Pritchett’s great work. {082-R01}

sections.label: The idea
sections.head: What the specialist can’t see
sections.caption: the invisible infrastructure
body: Good poli­cies, Ajay Shah said, do not travel well. A mil­i­tary af­fairs geek who loves the Norwegian mil­i­tary may want to bring over its man­u­als and its tac­tics, tech­niques and pro­ce­dures. An ad­mirer of TSMC may want to repli­cate it in Bombay. Neither, he said, would work.
Amit Varma said Shruti Rajagopalan and Alex Tabarrok had made much the same point in a paper whose title he nearly got rudely wrong: *Premature Imitation and India’s Flailing State*. {082-J02}
Varma reached for a bi­o­log­i­cal term, iso­mor­phic mimicry. Shah drew a dis­tinc­tion.
## Hollow or bro­ken

In mimicry, a harm­less moth wears the colours of a poi­sonous in­sect so that birds leave it alone. India’s ver­sion, Shah said, is a fancy build­ing called a the­atre com­mand, a cen­tral bank or a food safety reg­u­la­tor, with all the pomp, head­count and con­fer­ence rooms of its first-world name­sake, but none of the peo­ple, pro­cesses, checks and in­cen­tives.

Invisible-infrastructure fail­ure is dif­fer­ent. You hon­estly try to build a Bank of England in India, and it floun­ders any­way. “Here in­side it’s not empty, but it’s ac­tu­ally mal­func­tion­ing,” Shah said. {082-C02}
~ Varma sug­gested the two sit on a con­tin­uum. He also had a Hindi sum­mary of the hol­low kind: a cen­tral bank on the out­side, hol­low on the in­side.

quote.text: So here you have some­thing that doesn’t work in prac­tice, and so we should un­der­stand why it doesn’t work in the­ory.

sections.label: Three lenses
sections.head: When the call doesn’t return
sections.caption: institutions making API calls
body: Ajay Shah’s first lens came from soft­ware. Every in­sti­tu­tion makes de­mands on ca­pa­bil­i­ties else­where in the econ­omy, like an API call. When the French health­care sys­tem buys some­thing, it re­lies on prod­uct safety and li­a­bil­ity rules made by oth­ers. {082-C03}
In rich coun­tries the calls just work. Under un­der­de­vel­op­ment, he said, the ca­pa­bil­i­ties ei­ther don’t exist or you are “stand­ing on shift­ing sands” and the call is un­re­li­able.

Pensions are his ex­am­ple. India’s mil­i­tary re­forms got tripped up be­cause mil­i­tary pen­sions were not solved as part of wider pen­sion re­form. With a sound, econ­omy-wide de­fined con­tri­bu­tion sys­tem, Amit Varma said, the mil­i­tary would be like an ap­pli­ca­tion that plugs into it.
## Who watches the can­teen

The sec­ond lens is in­cen­tives. Nobody is a saint, and the sur­round­ings shape what peo­ple max­imise. A can­teen ven­dor in the Norwegian mil­i­tary, Shah said, is un­likely even to imag­ine cor­rup­tion in food pro­cure­ment. In India the con­di­tions are dif­fer­ent.
The third is checks and bal­ances, many of them in­her­ited. Every American fed­eral agency gets an in­spec­tor gen­eral, a sys­tem built over a hun­dred years. {082-C04}
~ Courts are a call too. Shah guessed a UK mal­prac­tice case is de­cided cor­rectly 80 per cent of the time. In India, he said, it is “al­most a coin toss”. {#coin}

quote.text: So think of that as an API call that each piece of the pol­icy ecosys­tem re­quires other pieces to work.

sections.label: What is to be done
sections.head: Five watts, one square micron
sections.caption: the trouble with specialisation
body: Ajay Shah named his plan after Lenin’s man­i­festo *What Is to Be Done*, hav­ing first quoted, tongue in cheek, “the great man Karl Marx”. With hind­sight, Amit Varma replied, it was what is not to be done. {082-J10}

The first item: be wary of spe­cial­i­sa­tion. Every in­cen­tive of the mod­ern world, Shah said, pushes peo­ple to dive deep, be­cause ex­per­tise earns re­spect. {082-C07} Narrow depth is the easy path and makes you less use­ful. Better to have breadth, and the horse­power to mas­ter any­thing in a cou­ple of weeks when needed.

Shah and a col­league once agreed, with a look, that STEM is easy and hu­man­i­ties is hard. By hu­man­i­ties, Varma said, they meant learn­ing the human con­di­tion through books, world cin­ema and music, not uni­ver­sity de­part­ments.
## Technician or thinker
Narrow depth, Shah said, makes you a tech­ni­cian, a cog in the wheel. Leaders like it: they want peo­ple who shut up and ex­e­cute. That suits the prin­ci­pal, not al­ways the agent. {082-C09}
Varma was blunter. Over-specialised peo­ple, he said, will have work got out of them for a while. “After that, they’ll get it done from AI.” {082-J15}
~ He gen­er­alised C.L.R. James: what do they know of X who only X know? Even depth, he said, needs breadth.

quote.text: The very essence of grow­ing is de­vel­op­ing breadth, is de­vel­op­ing strate­gic sense, is ris­ing from being a tech­ni­cian to being a thinker.

sections.label: Think locally
sections.head: Know the road at night
sections.caption: thinking locally
body: Before you trans­plant the French health­care sys­tem into Haryana, Ajay Shah said, you must be deeply grounded in Haryana. Can a truck car­ry­ing ex­pen­sive ma­te­ri­als travel at night on such and such road? Only some­one who lives there knows. {082-C10}
He called it au­then­tic­ity, “the beau­ti­ful hu­man­i­ties word”: being em­bed­ded in a cul­ture and a place, with a com­mon-sense in­tu­ition for how it works.

Amit Varma’s ex­am­ple was Sowmya Dhanaraj, whose episode of *The Seen and the Unseen* is in his top ten. Her par­ents worked in a fac­tory, and her mother sold tea at a stall on the Coimbatore Highway for many years. {082-S04}
## Rooted, not im­ported

Her ed­u­ca­tion was the same as ev­ery­one else’s, Varma said, but her think­ing comes from the bot­tom up, from the way India re­ally is. That bedrock, he said, will help her craft good pol­icy what­ever she does.
The warn­ing cuts both ways. Shah cau­tioned Indians who want to ex­port Indian suc­cesses to Morocco or Mozambique, where the in­vis­i­ble in­fra­struc­ture is very dif­fer­ent.
~ Earlier, Varma had sketched the op­po­site type: born priv­i­leged in a big city, ed­u­cated abroad, back with jar­gon and frames that don’t apply.

quote.text: She doesn’t have that elite ed­u­ca­tion. She doesn’t have for­eign ideas im­planted into her brain. She’s seen the world. She’s asked the right ques­tions.

sections.label: Do less
sections.head: The courage to walk away
sections.caption: the virtue of doing nothing
body: Ajay Shah con­fessed to being “a soft pinko”. In Sweden, with gov­ern­ment ex­pen­di­ture at some fifty-five per cent of GDP, it is hard not to be im­pressed. {#sweden}

But state ca­pa­bil­ity, he said, is a very fi­nite mus­cle. It should be lav­ished on a few prob­lems, and India should walk away from those that are un­rea­son­ably dif­fi­cult or im­pos­si­ble in its con­di­tions.
His ex­am­ple was de­fined ben­e­fit pen­sions. The cor­rect an­swer, Shah said, is “four hun­dred years more until India be­comes an ad­vanced econ­omy”. {#fourhundred}
## Rich first
Amit Varma drew on Johan Norberg: Scandinavian coun­tries grew rich through free mar­kets and en­trepreneur­ship, and built wel­fare states only af­ter­wards, while keep­ing busi­ness easy. {082-R14}

Lant Pritchett’s paper, Varma said, shows a ninety-nine per cent cor­re­la­tion be­tween human wel­fare in­di­ca­tors and per capita GDP. Get the growth first, he ar­gued, and re­dis­tribute once the pie is big enough. {082-C12}
India, Varma said, does many things badly in­stead of a few things well. Every in­ter­ven­tion also has an op­por­tu­nity cost: spend money here, and the state can’t spend it some­where else.
~ A mar­ket fail­ure, Varma added, is nec­es­sary for the state to act but not suf­fi­cient. Famines, hu­man­i­tar­ian crises and pol­lu­tion qual­ify; small stuff does not.

quote.text: Many, many times the wise an­swer is to shrink the scope of the Indian state.

sections.label: Fix the foundations
sections.head: Rocket first, payload later
sections.caption: the rocket and the payload
body: Ajay Shah’s last item was to work on foun­da­tions: the legal sys­tem, the rule of law, gov­ern­ment HR and con­tract­ing, and checks on the state’s co­er­cive power. “Coercive power is a poi­son,” he said.

In the book he wrote with Vijay Kelkar, *In Service of the Republic*, there is a rocket and pay­load anal­ogy. Take the cen­tral sta­tis­ti­cal or­gan­i­sa­tion. The pay­load is GDP mea­sure­ment and ques­tions like dou­ble de­fla­tion. The bulk of the or­gan­i­sa­tion, its bud­get­ing, pub­lic fi­nan­cial man­age­ment, con­tract­ing and HR, is the rocket.
If the rocket fails, he said, there is no point being a sub­ject mat­ter ex­pert on dou­ble de­fla­tion.
## Everyone’s prob­lem

So fewer peo­ple should work on one do­main and more on what cuts across all of them. A nar­row spe­cial­ist wants to run AIIMS prop­erly. Someone who wants a more con­se­quen­tial life goes after gov­ern­ment HR, be­cause it is ev­ery­where. {082-C14}
All these, he said, are high im­pact, be­cause they help all the sec­tors.
~ Amit Varma tested the idea with a clumsy anal­ogy of his own: toi­lets built under Swachh Bharat with no drainage. {082-S05}

quote.text: If we fix gov­ern­ment HR all across the land­scape, we will get hun­dreds of bet­ter func­tion­ing gov­ern­ment agen­cies.

Don’t say no­bil­ity, pa­tri­o­tism, those are all bad rea­sons. Think deeply about in­cen­tives. Why do peo­ple be­have the way they be­have, and that will take you to the in­vis­i­ble in­fra­struc­ture.

p3.title: Tales of the unseen
p3.deck: Four stories of systems nobody noticed until they went missing

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the system where the light bulb went off
stories.head: No French cure for India
body: Ajay Shah says the idea of in­vis­i­ble in­fra­struc­ture clicked for him while study­ing one sys­tem: French health­care. “For me per­son­ally, that was where some light bulb went off,” he said.

Rich coun­tries have many prob­lems in their health­care sys­tems, most no­tably the United States, which he said prob­a­bly spends three times as much as other OECD coun­tries and gets much worse out­comes. {#threex}

France is dif­fer­ent. Its ar­range­ment of pub­lic and pri­vate works rather well. Anyone with an in­ter­est in health, Shah said, will in­evitably dig deeper, and then won­der whether India could have the same.

That is where the mis­take lies. “The mis­take around in­vis­i­ble in­fra­struc­ture would be to start think­ing that be­cause XYZ de­sign of the French health­care sys­tem works so well in France, we could or should trans­plant that into India,” he said. {082-S01}

French health­care, Shah ar­gued, sits on a base of a hun­dred other sub­sys­tems: bud­get­ing, the rule of law and its en­force­ment, prod­uct li­a­bil­ity and li­a­bil­ity in health­care, the government’s HR and con­tract­ing, the be­hav­iour of pub­lic and pri­vate. Each ex­erts tugs and pulls on the sys­tem.
None of this is hid­den, he said: any­one who both­ers to look can see the French courts and the government’s con­tract­ing. But spe­cial­ists tend to be blind to them. {082-C01}
~ So health­care peo­ple talk to health­care peo­ple. The NHS is good at one thing, the French at an­other; each should steal the other’s ideas. Then, sure enough, the trans­plants work pretty badly.
stories.why: A suc­cess­ful in­sti­tu­tion is the vis­i­ble top of a large stack of sup­port­ing sys­tems. The specialist’s depth keeps that stack out of view, which is why the ex­pert is often the one propos­ing a trans­plant that fails.
stories.postscript: For all his study, Shah ad­mit­ted, he has not yet had a chance to visit France.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the French healthcare system

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on an American rule that keeps police in check
stories.head: Tap illegally, lose the case
body: Suppose a law says a po­lice­man needs a judge’s war­rant be­fore tap­ping your phone, Ajay Shah said. She taps it any­way, and finds proof that you are the mur­derer.

In the United States, he be­lieves, judges set­tled this in 1938 with a bright-line test, the fruit of the poi­sonous tree doc­trine: ev­i­dence ob­tained through il­le­gal means is in­ad­mis­si­ble. {#y1938}

Without it, he ar­gued, po­lice would never bother with war­rants. If they found noth­ing, they would at least have black­mail ma­te­rial; if they found some­thing, the ends would jus­tify the means. {082-S02}

~ Amit Varma added a sec­ond safe­guard: in­ves­ti­ga­tors and pros­e­cu­tors sit in sep­a­rate de­part­ments, and pros­e­cu­tors judged on suc­cess­ful pros­e­cu­tions won’t take weak cases. Shah noted that India has nei­ther.

quote.text: If il­le­gally ob­tained ev­i­dence is per­mis­si­ble in court, why would a cop ever take the per­mis­sion?

stories.postscript: Anyone who has watched *Chicago PD* or *Law and Order*, Amit Varma said, knows ev­i­dence from an il­le­gal search is not ad­mis­si­ble. {082-J06}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the fruit of the poisonous tree

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a sanitation drive that forgot the drains
stories.head: A toilet with nowhere to go
body: Amit Varma re­called a point Shruti Rajagopalan made on his show *The Seen and the Unseen*. Under Swachh Bharat, toi­lets went up in vil­lages all over the place, but often with no drainage sys­tem.
People in higher-caste houses would not touch their own refuse, so they got peo­ple from lower castes to do the job. The scheme, Varma said, ex­ac­er­bated the caste sys­tem. {082-S05}

Ajay Shah was in­dig­nant. “What kind of water and san­i­ta­tion per­son are you if you think that there’ll be toi­let but you haven’t thought through how the water will come and how the sewage will go out?” {082-J18}
~ “This was not my de­ci­sion,” Varma said. Drainage was vis­i­ble, Shah ob­jected. Things like drainage, water and elec­tric­ity, Varma replied, be­come in­vis­i­ble be­cause we nor­malise them.
stories.why: Every in­ter­ven­tion, even a toi­let, de­pends on sys­tems around it: water com­ing in, sewage going out. Leave them out, and the fix can make the orig­i­nal prob­lem worse, as the toi­lets did for caste.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Swachh Bharat toilets

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on aid that assumed the power was on
stories.head: Cool comfort for Latur
body: After the Latur earth­quake, Amit Varma re­mem­bers, Japan sent some four hun­dred air con­di­tion­ers as re­lief. {082-S06}
Most of those places didn’t even have elec­tric­ity, he said, and even if they had, the sur­vivors would not have needed air con­di­tion­ers. It was “com­pletely out of whack”.

Varma of­fered it as part of what he called a clumsy anal­ogy. Any busi­ness, whether a fac­tory, a ser­vices firm or a restau­rant, makes API calls to water sup­ply and elec­tric­ity. {#apicalls} We nor­malise such things until they turn in­vis­i­ble.
~ And seen from the sky-high dis­tance of an elite Ivy League ed­u­ca­tion, he said, “you can just nor­mal­ize and as­sume it is there and things can go wrong.”

quote.text: Japan sent some four hun­dred air con­di­tion­ers or some­thing as re­lief. Which makes ab­so­lutely no sense, right?

quiz.q: What, by Ajay Shah’s guess, is the chance a UK malpractice case is decided correctly?
quiz.a: About 80 per cent; in India, he said, it is al­most a coin toss.

quiz.q: Under which American doctrine is evidence from an illegal phone tap thrown out of court?
quiz.a: The fruit of the poi­sonous tree doc­trine, which Shah be­lieves dates from 1938.

quiz.q: Whose analogy likens a twenty-year Bank of England veteran to a New York taxi driver?
quiz.a: Lant Pritchett’s: such prac­ti­tion­ers know the how of pol­icy, but not the why.

quiz.q: What did Japan send as relief after the Latur earthquake, as Amit Varma recalls?
quiz.a: Some four hun­dred air con­di­tion­ers, to places that mostly had no elec­tric­ity.

quiz.q: In the Kelkar and Shah book, what is the rocket and what is the payload?
quiz.a: The pay­load is do­main work like GDP mea­sure­ment; the rocket is HR, bud­get­ing, con­tract­ing.

quiz.q: From which song, and by whom, did *Everything is Everything* take its name?
quiz.a: Bruce Springsteen’s *You’re Missing*; John Lennon’s *Watching the Wheels* was the run­ner-up.

glossary.def: Copying the out­ward look of an in­sti­tu­tion with­out its work­ing in­sides.
A re­quest one sys­tem makes to ca­pa­bil­i­ties an­other pro­vides.
Assuming no­body is a saint and ask­ing what each actor max­imises.
A pen­sion promis­ing set pay­outs, which Shah says India should not at­tempt.
Mildly left-leaning, as Ajay Shah de­scribed him­self in prais­ing Sweden.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 82. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Bruce Springsteen (Raph_PH, CC BY 4.0); Johan Norberg (Krubaston, CC0); John Lennon (Jack Mitchell, CC BY-SA 3.0).

shelf.title: Premature Imitation and India’s Flailing State
shelf.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan and Alexander Tabarrok
shelf.why: A ‘great paper’ on why India copies the forms of ad­vanced-economy pol­icy from Britain, the US or Sweden too early and ends up with a flail­ing state, build­ing on Lant Pritchett’s idea of iso­mor­phic mimicry.

shelf.title: Elite Imitation in Public Policy (Episode 180 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Alex Tabarrok
shelf.why: Shruti Rajagopalan and Alex Tabarrok on why poli­cies that Indian elites copy from abroad fail in India: a long con­ver­sa­tion about their pre­ma­ture-imitation the­sis.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: Understanding India’s Pensions Disaster (Episode 65)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A first-principles ac­count of pen­sion re­form: how a small com­mu­nity with a shared phi­los­o­phy built the NPS, and how guar­an­tees and the old mess re­turned once that com­mu­nity dis­persed and its knowl­edge faded.

shelf.title: The Horrors of KYC (Episode 74)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The case that India’s KYC regime has mainly built mass sur­veil­lance of citizens’ fi­nances while never stop­ping a ter­ror­ist plot, and that the real dan­ger is a state watch­ing cit­i­zens and turn­ing its co­er­cive power on them.

shelf.title: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Explains that politi­cians and bu­reau­crats re­spond to in­cen­tives like ev­ery­one else, so the state is no benev­o­lent beast and gov­ern­ment fail­ure is far more com­mon than mar­ket fail­ure.

shelf.title: Stay Away From Luxury Beliefs (Episode 46)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: On be­liefs im­ported from rich-world dis­course that make their hold­ers feel vir­tu­ous while hurt­ing the peo­ple they claim to help, such as the min­i­mum wage, or op­pos­ing sweat­shops that beat every other op­tion work­ers have.

shelf.title: India’s Problem is Poverty, Not Inequality
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit sep­a­rates two prob­lems peo­ple rou­tinely con­fuse and that need op­po­site so­lu­tions: in a pos­i­tive-sum world in­equal­ity can rise while poverty falls, as in India after 1991, so end­ing poverty through growth is the real moral im­per­a­tive.

shelf.title: Ajay Shah Brings the Dreams of the 20th Century (Episode 402 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A ten-and-a-half-hour con­ver­sa­tion with Ajay about his life and ideas, in­clud­ing the in­side story of how India built a good eq­uity mar­ket through SEBI, NSE and NSDL.

shelf.title: Watching the Wheels
shelf.creator: John Lennon
shelf.why: A song both hosts love and the run­ner-up name for the pod­cast: con­tem­pla­tive and hum­ble, the uni­verse trundling along while we watch, cu­ri­ous and amused.

shelf.title: You’re Missing
shelf.creator: Bruce Springsteen
shelf.why: The Springsteen song that gave the show its name and world­view: its line ‘ev­ery­thing is everything’ points at all the world’s won­ders while mark­ing someone’s ab­sence.

shelf.title: Life Lessons From Chess in 2024 (Episode 81)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Lessons from chess on why re­newal mat­ters more than mas­tery (ex­perts in nar­row fields stop learn­ing), why young play­ers peak in a fi­nite game, and why a great firm re­cruits from all over the world.

shelf.title: Sowmya Dhanaraj Is Making a Difference (Episode 380 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Sowmya Dhanaraj
shelf.why: One of Amit’s ten favourite episodes: econ­o­mist Sowmya Dhanaraj, whose par­ents were fac­tory work­ers and whose mother sold tea on the Coimbatore high­way, ques­tions re­ceived wis­dom from lived Indian re­al­ity rather than im­ported frame­works.

shelf.title: Johan Norberg’s books and videos
shelf.creator: Johan Norberg
shelf.why: Norberg shows that Scandinavia grew rich through free mar­kets and en­trepreneur­ship first and added the wel­fare state only after be­com­ing ad­vanced economies.

shelf.title: Economic growth is enough and only economic growth is enough
shelf.creator: Lant Pritchett with Addison Lewis
shelf.why: Pritchett’s paper, which Amit calls a mas­ter­piece of data and clear lan­guage, finds that human wel­fare in­di­ca­tors from health on­wards cor­re­late at around 99% with per capita GDP, leav­ing re­dis­tri­bu­tion and wel­farism a sliver of the story.

shelf.title: Understanding the State (Episode 25 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The foun­da­tion of the show’s think­ing on gov­ern­ment: the state is a mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence that acts through co­er­cion, so every in­ter­ven­tion, paid for by taxes, must be jus­ti­fied.

shelf.title: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on mar­ket fail­ure in its pre­cise tech­ni­cal sense (pub­lic goods, ex­ter­nal­i­ties and the rest) and on the nar­row con­di­tions under which the state may in­ter­vene, con­di­tions that are nec­es­sary but not suf­fi­cient.

shelf.title: Swachh Bharat (Episode 82 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan
shelf.why: Shows how a well-intentioned scheme that ig­nored its sup­port­ing in­fra­struc­ture ended up re­in­forc­ing caste prac­tices.

shelf.title: Life Lessons
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit and Ajay’s course on what they wish they had been taught at twenty: learn­ing how to learn, frame­works for think­ing, writ­ing, prob­a­bilis­tic in­tu­ition, eco­nom­ics, the his­tory of thought, per­sonal fi­nance (Ajay’s mod­ule is ‘legendary’) and health.

laughs.text: Amit’s open­ing: ‘Welcome to Everything Is Everything and wel­come to the Seen and the Unseen. And no, this is not a cross­over episode,’ since the episode is all about un­seen things.

Amit nam­ing Shruti Rajagopalan and Alex Tabarrok’s paper: ‘They did this great paper called Premature uh I was about to say ejac­u­la­tion. That’s not the name of the… Premature Imitation and the Flailing State.’

Ajay in­verts the old econ­o­mist joke: ‘An econ­o­mist is some­one who, when some­thing works in prac­tice, won­ders whether it works in the­ory. So here you have some­thing that doesn’t work in prac­tice, and so we should un­der­stand why it doesn’t work in the­ory.’
Amit sums up iso­mor­phic mimicry in Hindi: ‘Bahar se cen­tral bank, andar se khokhla’, mean­ing a cen­tral bank on the out­side, hol­low on the in­side.

Ajay quotes ‘the great man Karl Marx’ (the tomb­stone line about philoso­phers and chang­ing the world). Amit quickly tells lis­ten­ers it’s tongue-in-cheek and that both think Marx’s ideas were dev­as­tat­ing: ‘Groucho Marx is great, but you’ve got to be care­ful.’
Ajay names his ac­tion plan after Lenin’s man­i­festo ‘What is to be done’. Amit replies: ‘with hind­sight we know is what is not to be done.’
Amit teas­ing Ajay: ‘I know you have depth in eight sub­jects you are happy to talk about and eight more you will not re­veal to the pub­lic.’
Amit on spe­cial­ists: ‘they’ll get work done out of you for a while. After that, they’ll get it done from AI.’
Isomorphic mimicry from bi­ol­ogy: a harm­less moth wears a poi­sonous insect’s colours so birds won’t eat it. Ajay ap­plies it to Indian agen­cies that copy the look of first-world in­sti­tu­tions.
Post-1945 Germany: Ajay de­scribes the ef­fort, across the OECD and most of all in Germany, to pro­tect in­di­vid­u­als ‘even if a Hitler would win a fu­ture elec­tion a la 1933.’

C.L.R. James’s ‘What do they know of cricket, who only cricket know’, which Amit notes was it­self a riff on Rudyard Kipling’s ‘what do they know of Britain who only Britain know.’ Amit ends with his own twist: ‘what do they know of depth only depth know.’
Bob Dylan’s line, cited by Amit for life­long re­newal: if you’re not busy being born, you’re busy dying.
